question: arXiv:1005.5480v3 tests the uniformity of the Fermi bubble spectrum by splitting the bubble template into a north and a south bubble, and it also repeats the template fit with the Haslam 408 MHz map in place of the simple disk model as the inverse-Compton template. In the north–south split of the fit that uses the simple disk model as the inverse-Compton template, which of the two bubbles comes out with the slightly harder spectrum, and to what does the paper attribute this? Why is the Haslam map not an ideal tracer of the inverse-Compton emission, and how does the fitted bubble spectrum change when it is used?

arguments.answer:
In the north–south split using the simple disk model as the IC template, the north bubble comes out slightly harder than the south bubble. The paper attributes this to including the Loop I template (which has a softer spectrum) in the northern sky in the regression fit. Both bubbles still have harder spectra than every other component in the fit.

The Haslam 408 MHz map is not an ideal IC tracer for two reasons. It contains a bright Loop I feature. It is also dominated by synchrotron emission from softer electron cosmic rays, with energies around 1 GeV, whereas IC emission depends on both the electron distribution and the interstellar radiation field.

With Haslam as the IC template, the best-fit bubble spectrum is still harder than the other components. The lower-energy (≲2 GeV) correlation coefficients are enhanced compared with the simple-disk and Fermi 0.5–1 GeV template fits.
